name: गुणत्रयविभागयोग
teaching: All of nature is woven of three strands: sattva binds with clarity and the pride of knowing, rajas with craving and restlessness, tamas with heaviness and sleep. Even goodness is a golden chain. Freedom is not perfecting the weave but seeing the weave — knowing the guṇas move among the guṇas while the witness stands apart. Three strands weave every mood, meal, and motive — naming them is half the freedom. The exit is not war against the weave but devotion to its Lord, who declares Himself the very foundation of Brahman.
questions: Which strand dominated your last twenty-four hours — clarity, agitation, or dullness?
How does your sattva bind you — what subtle pride rides on your discipline or insight?
The one beyond the guṇas 'neither hates their presence nor longs for their absence.' Can you let today's mood simply move through?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
परं भूयः प्रवक्ष्यामि ज्ञानानां ज्ञानमुत्तमम् ।
यज्ज्ञात्वा मुनयः सर्वे परां सिद्धिमितो गताः॥
verses.transliteration:
paraṃ bhūyaḥ pravakṣyāmi jñānānāṃ jñānamuttamam
yajjñātvā munayaḥ sarve parāṃ siddhimito gatāḥ
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: again I shall declare the supreme knowledge, best of all knowledges, knowing which all the sages have gone from here to the highest perfection.
verses.translation: I will again declare (to thee) that supreme knowledge, the best of all knowledge, having known which all the sages have gone to the supreme perfection after this life.

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, accusative singular (agrees with ज्ञानम्)
noun, feminine, accusative singular (goal of motion)

verses.explanation: Unprompted — no question from Arjuna this time — Krishna volunteers another summit: jñānānāṁ jñānam uttamam, the best of all knowings. Its credential is historical: every sage who ever left this place for perfection traveled by it. The subject will turn out to be the three strands every mind is woven from.
verses.connection: Opens the guna-analysis: ch13 mapped field and knower; ch14 maps the field's three threads.
verses.reflection: Receive the unprompted teaching today — wisdom that arrives before you knew to ask for it.
verses.background: Krishna volunteers a further depth: I shall declare again the supreme knowledge by which sages have gone from here to perfection — and frames all becoming as a cosmic conception: the great Brahman is My womb, in it I place the seed; from that comes the birth of all beings, whatever the womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
verses.hook: What knowledge did the sages know that carried them to perfection?

views.text: "Of all knowledges" means knowledge of things like sacrifice, which cannot free anyone; this knowledge alone leads to liberation, so it is praised as supreme and best to wake the listener's interest.
Takes this as another kind of knowledge, distinct from the earlier teaching on Prakṛti and the self; by it meditating sages reached the pure form of the self beyond saṃsāra.
The same knowledge as before, now unfolded in detail so each strand can be examined on its own; "by knowing which" vouches for its tested reliability.
Opens a chapter meant to deny that spirit and nature act on their own: their union, and the variety of saṃsāra it produces, happens by the Lord's will, not as godless Sāṅkhya holds.

Having shown that all life is soul joined with matter under God's direction, Krishna now opens a detailed teaching on the three qualities of nature, which, once realized, lifts one to the highest perfection.

verses.devanagari:
इदं ज्ञानमुपाश्रित्य मम साधर्म्यमागताः ।
सर्गेऽपि नोपजायन्ते प्रलये न व्यथन्ति च॥
verses.transliteration:
idaṃ jñānamupāśritya mama sādharmyamāgatāḥ
sarge'pi nopajāyante pralaye na vyathanti ca
verses.essence: Taking refuge in this knowledge, having come to share my own nature, they are not born even at a new creation, nor troubled at the dissolution.
verses.translation: They who, having taken refuge in this knowledge, have attained to unity with Me, are neither born at the time of creation nor are they disturbed at the time of dissolution.

anvaya.base: सर्ग · creation, emission of a world
anvaya.form: noun, masculine, locative singular (at the time of)
noun, masculine, locative singular (at the time of)
verb, present, 3rd person plural (irregular active form)

verses.explanation: The stakes, stated cosmically: mama sādharmyam — coming to share his very nature, read by some as identity, by others as likeness. Such knowers stand outside the universe's own heartbeat: when worlds are exhaled they are not re-embodied; when worlds are inhaled they do not flinch. Guna-knowledge, fully ripened, exempts one from the cosmic calendar itself.
verses.connection: Prices the knowledge of 14.1: beyond rebirth, beyond even the rebirth of universes.
verses.reflection: Aim high enough tonight: a knowing that stands calm even while worlds are exhaled and inhaled.
verses.background: Krishna volunteers a further depth: I shall declare again the supreme knowledge by which sages have gone from here to perfection — and frames all becoming as a cosmic conception: the great Brahman is My womb, in it I place the seed; from that comes the birth of all beings, whatever the womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
verses.hook: Can knowledge free you from being born again at each new creation?

views.text: Sādharmya means identity with the Lord's real nature, not similarity of attributes, since the Gita admits no difference between the knower of the field and God; the promised result is praise of the knowledge.
The knowers come to partake of the Lord's nature and attain his status: they are not drawn into the process of creation and escape the distress of dissolution.
Notes that vyathanti is an irregular, Vedic-style active form, and that similar irregular endings elsewhere in the Gita are to be explained the same way.
Those who live this knowledge escape rebirth and the dormant state at cosmic dissolution; freed from material energy, the soul comes under God's divine energy and takes on his godlike nature.

verses.devanagari:
मम योनिर्महद् ब्रह्म तस्मिन्गर्भं दधाम्यहम् ।
सम्भवः सर्वभूतानां ततो भवति भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
mama yonirmahad brahma tasmingarbhaṃ dadhāmyaham
sambhavaḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ tato bhavati bhārata
verses.essence: My womb is the great Brahman; in that I place the seed. From that, Bharata, comes the origin of all beings.
verses.translation: My womb is the great Brahma; in that I place the germ; thence, O Arjuna, is the birth of all beings.

anvaya.base: ब्रह्मन् · the vast; here primal nature

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being): "all beings"

verses.explanation: Creation as conception: mahad brahma — vast nature herself — as womb, and Krishna as the one who plants the garbha, the seed of consciousness. The metaphor honors both parents: matter is not dead stuff awaiting a command but the great mother; spirit is not a distant architect but the intimate father. Every being is their child.
verses.connection: The cosmology behind 13.27's field-knower union: the marriage now imaged as parenthood.
verses.reflection: Honor both your parents in everything today: matter the great womb, spirit the seed.
verses.background: Krishna volunteers a further depth: I shall declare again the supreme knowledge by which sages have gone from here to perfection — and frames all becoming as a cosmic conception: the great Brahman is My womb, in it I place the seed; from that comes the birth of all beings, whatever the womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
verses.hook: How does Krishna describe the birth of all living beings?

refs.note: The Lord places souls in the womb of material nature, which then shapes bodies for them according to their karmas, as this verse describes.

views.text: The womb is the Lord's own māyā, prakṛti of three guṇas, called 'great' as greater than its effects and 'brahma' as sustaining them; placing the seed means joining the field with its knower, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha's birth.
'Great brahman' is non-conscient prakṛti, so named as cause of Mahat and the rest; the seed is his higher prakṛti, the mass of conscious selves, which he lays in it by his will.
The mighty Brahman is the Lord's own expansive energy; holding that energy of Self-consciousness, he moves the tiny souls through birth and death as an act of favour.

Prakṛti and the souls cause beings only under the Lord, never on their own: at creation he rejoins the soul that lay merged in him, still carrying ignorance, desire and karma, with the field it will experience.
Material nature is like a womb into which God places the souls turned away from him; nature then creates bodies for them according to their past karmas.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वयोनिषु कौन्तेय मूर्तयः सम्भवन्ति याः ।
तासां ब्रह्म महद्योनिरहं बीजप्रदः पिता॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvayoniṣu kaunteya mūrtayaḥ sambhavanti yāḥ
tāsāṃ brahma mahadyonirahaṃ bījapradaḥ pitā
verses.essence: Whatever forms arise in all wombs, Kaunteya — the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
verses.translation: Whatever forms are produced, O Arjuna, in any womb whatsoever, the great Brahma is their womb and I am the seed-giving father.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + योनि (womb): "all wombs"

anvaya.base: ब्रह्मन् · the vast; here primal nature

anvaya.parts: बीज (seed) + प्रद (giver): "one who gives the seed"

verses.explanation: The claim universalized: sarva-yoniṣu, *all* wombs — moth, mongoose, monarch, god. One mother, one father, behind every birth in every species; the family of beings is literal, not poetic. For Arjuna, facing 'enemies', the genealogy is pointed: everyone on that field has the same two parents he does.
verses.connection: Extends 14.3 to every species — the metaphysical ground of universal kinship.
verses.reflection: Greet one creature of another species today as family — same mother, same father, truly.
verses.background: Krishna volunteers a further depth: I shall declare again the supreme knowledge by which sages have gone from here to perfection — and frames all becoming as a cosmic conception: the great Brahman is My womb, in it I place the seed; from that comes the birth of all beings, whatever the womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
verses.hook: Who is the father of every form of life, in every womb?

refs.note: Describes the Supreme Lord impregnating material nature with souls, matching the image of God as seed-giving father.

views.text: 'Great Brahman' is glossed as the great sustainer that exists as all the various forms; it is the womb of every body born from gods, manes, humans or beasts, and God is the father who deposits the seed.
In every womb, of gods, Gandharvas, humans or animals, prakṛti holding the selves he has placed in it is the cause; he is the sowing father who places each self according to its karma.
The Lord's expansive energy is present in every womb as the Mother who brings forth the whole world-process; he himself is the Father, the bearer of that energy, beyond description.
This is not only how beings arose at the start of creation: births in every species, moving and unmoving, always come about this way, from prakṛti as mother and the Lord as father.
God is the father who casts the souls into nature, the mother; only those who have turned away from him are sent into the material world.

verses.devanagari:
सत्त्वं रजस्तम इति गुणाः प्रकृतिसम्भवाः ।
निबध्नन्ति महाबाहो देहे देहिनमव्ययम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sattvaṃ rajastama iti guṇāḥ prakṛtisambhavāḥ
nibadhnanti mahābāho dehe dehinamavyayam
verses.essence: Sattva, rajas, tamas — these gunas, born of prakriti, bind the imperishable embodied one in the body, Mahabaho.
verses.translation: Purity, passion and inertia these qualities, O Arjuna, born of Nature, bind fast in the body, the embodied, the indestructible.

anvaya.base: सत्त्व · being, purity, the bright strand
thus; marks a list or quotation

anvaya.parts: प्रकृति (nature) + सम्भव (origin): "whose origin is prakriti"
महा (great) + बाहु (arm): "one whose arms are mighty"

anvaya.base: देहिन् · one who has a body, the soul

verses.explanation: The chapter's three protagonists enter: luminous sattva, restless rajas, heavy tamas — guna literally meaning 'strand' or 'rope.' The paradox is stated whole: they bind the avyayam, the *changeless*, the imperishable. How does rope hold what can never be touched? Only 'as it were', by persuasion, the next verses show — each strand binds with a different bait.
verses.connection: Names the three ropes; 14.6–8 will examine each knot.
verses.reflection: Learn your three ropes by name today: sattva, rajas, tamas — you cannot loosen what you cannot name.
verses.background: The three strands are introduced by name and grip: sattva, rajas, tamas, born of prakriti, binding the imperishable dweller in the body — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by thirst and attachment to action, tamas by negligence, sloth, and sleep, veiling knowledge.
verses.hook: What ties the deathless self down to the body?

views.text: Guṇa is a technical term, not a quality inhering in a substance; being forms of ignorance, the strands bind the changeless Self only 'as it were', which answers how the untainted one of 13.31 can be bound.
The guṇas are known only through effects like brightness and show only in prakṛti's evolutes; the self is not tied to them by nature but is bound while it dwells in a body.
The Mother binds the embodied soul with her three strands for the sake of his enjoyment, a binding that lasts until his emancipation.
The soul is divine but, identifying with a body made of nature, it is coloured by whichever of the three qualities dominates, like a print taking the hue of the ink used most.

verses.devanagari:
तत्र सत्त्वं निर्मलत्वात्प्रकाशकमनामयम् ।
सुखसङ्गेन बध्नाति ज्ञानसङ्गेन चानघ॥
verses.transliteration:
tatra sattvaṃ nirmalatvātprakāśakamanāmayam
sukhasaṅgena badhnāti jñānasaṅgena cānagha
verses.essence: Of these, sattva — stainless, luminous, free of affliction — binds by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge, sinless one.
verses.translation: Of these, Sattva, which from its stainlessness is luminous and healthy, binds by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge, O sinless one.

anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + आमय (disease): "having no disease"

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: सुख (happiness) + सङ्ग (attachment): "attachment to happiness"

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + सङ्ग (attachment): "attachment to knowledge"
अन् (not) + अघ (sin): "one without sin"

verses.explanation: The subtlest trap first: sattva, everything one would want — clear, bright, healthy — and still a rope. Its baits are the finest available: sukha-saṅga, the clinging to feeling good, and jñāna-saṅga, the clinging to *being the one who knows*. A golden chain is the teaching's classic gloss: beautiful, comfortable, and still a chain.
verses.connection: The first knot examined — and the chapter's hardest lesson: even the best quality binds.
verses.reflection: Inspect even your virtues tonight: where has feeling-good, or being-the-one-who-knows, become a chain?
verses.background: The three strands are introduced by name and grip: sattva, rajas, tamas, born of prakriti, binding the imperishable dweller in the body — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by thirst and attachment to action, tamas by negligence, sloth, and sleep, veiling knowledge.
verses.hook: How can even goodness and happiness keep you bound?

views.text: The thought 'I am happy' joins an object's quality to the subject, which is nescience; the knowledge meant here belongs to the inner organ, not the Self, otherwise there could be no bondage through it.
Sattva produces knowledge and happiness and then attachment to them; that attachment drives secular and Vedic efforts to secure them, and so births in bodies suited to those fruits.
A golden fetter: the sattvic person compares himself with others, grows proud of his learning and comfort, and thinks 'I am happy, I am wise'.
Goodness brings calm, health and knowledge, yet attachment to it still binds; like a robber who frees you but cannot leave the forest, it shows the way out but must itself be transcended.

verses.devanagari:
रजो रागात्मकं विद्धि तृष्णासङ्गसमुद्भवम् ।
तन्निबध्नाति कौन्तेय कर्मसङ्गेन देहिनम्॥
verses.transliteration:
rajo rāgātmakaṃ viddhi tṛṣṇāsaṅgasamudbhavam
tannibadhnāti kaunteya karmasaṅgena dehinam
verses.essence: Know rajas to be of the nature of passion, the source of craving and clinging; it binds the embodied one, Kaunteya, by attachment to action.
verses.translation: Know thou Rajas to be of the nature of passion, the source of thirst (for sensual enjoyment) and attachment; it binds fast, O Arjuna, the embodied one by attachment to action.

anvaya.base: रागात्मक · having passion as its nature
anvaya.parts: राग (passion, colouring) + आत्मक (having the nature of): "whose nature is passion"

anvaya.base: तृष्णासङ्गसमुद्भव · source of thirst and attachment
anvaya.parts: तृष्णा (thirst) + सङ्ग (attachment) + समुद्भव (origin): "from which thirst and attachment arise" (also read: arising from them)

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + सङ्ग (attachment): "attachment to action"

anvaya.base: देहिन् · one who has a body

verses.explanation: The middle strand: rajas, pure momentum — tṛṣṇā, the thirst that drinking only sharpens, and saṅga, the grip. Its rope is karma-saṅga: addiction not to any particular outcome but to *doing itself*, the itch that makes stillness feel like dying. Most of what the world calls ambition is this strand, holding the leash.
verses.connection: The second knot: the restless rope behind 3.5's truth that no one rests a moment without acting.
verses.reflection: Catch the thirst that drinking sharpens once today — and skip one round of feeding it.
verses.background: The three strands are introduced by name and grip: sattva, rajas, tamas, born of prakriti, binding the imperishable dweller in the body — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by thirst and attachment to action, tamas by negligence, sloth, and sleep, veiling knowledge.
verses.hook: How does passion keep a person tied to endless activity?

refs.note: Patañjali's system names activity as passion's chief expression, while this verse names attachment and desire.

views.text: Rāga comes from 'colouring', like ochre dye; tṛṣṇā is longing for what one lacks, saṅga clinging to what one has; rajas binds through deep involvement in actions for seen and unseen ends.
Takes rāga as desire between man and woman and saṅga as longing for sons and friends; actions begun out of such longing become the cause of new births.
Desire fed is like petrol poured on fire: the rajasic person is never content, and rajas plants the idea 'I am the doer' in the silent witness.
Passion and desire feed each other, driving restless pursuit of status, wealth and family; offering the fruits of one's work to God breaks the cycle and calms passion.

verses.devanagari:
तमस्त्वज्ञानजं विद्धि मोहनं सर्वदेहिनाम् ।
प्रमादालस्यनिद्राभिस्तन्निबध्नाति भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
tamastvajñānajaṃ viddhi mohanaṃ sarvadehinām
pramādālasyanidrābhistannibadhnāti bhārata
verses.essence: But know tamas as born of ignorance, deluding all embodied beings; it binds, Bharata, with negligence, laziness and sleep.
verses.translation: But know thou Tamas to be born of ignorance, deluding all embodied beings; it binds fast, O Arjuna, by heedlessness, indolence and sleep.

anvaya.parts: अज्ञान (ignorance) + ज (born): "born of ignorance"
सर्व (all) + देहिन् (embodied one): "all the embodied"

anvaya.form: noun compound, feminine, instrumental plural (by means of)
anvaya.parts: प्रमाद (negligence) + आलस्य (laziness) + निद्रा (sleep): a list joined by 'and'

verses.explanation: The heaviest strand: tamas, darkness as a force — not the absence of energy but an active mohanam, a deluding fog. Its three ropes need no bait at all: pramāda, the slow leak of carelessness; ālasya, the body's refusal; nidrā, sleep beyond the body's need. Where rajas binds by motion, tamas binds by weight.
verses.connection: The third knot completes the set — three ropes, three entirely different grips.
verses.reflection: Name tamas honestly where you find it today: the fog, the heaviness, the not-caring — naming thins it.
verses.background: The three strands are introduced by name and grip: sattva, rajas, tamas, born of prakriti, binding the imperishable dweller in the body — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by thirst and attachment to action, tamas by negligence, sloth, and sleep, veiling knowledge.
verses.hook: What does the quality of darkness do to a person?

views.text: Tamas, the third quality, deludes all embodied beings as a cause of indiscrimination; born of ignorance, it binds them through inadvertence, laziness and sleep.

Ajñāna here is knowledge contrary to how things are, and delusion is erroneous knowledge; negligence leads to doing what should not be done, indolence avoids work, and sleep is the senses resting from exhaustion.
Pramāda is wasting the rare human birth, won by long merit and the only means to emancipation; laziness means sloth in doing good.
Each of the three ropes opposes something: negligence blocks sattva's discrimination, laziness blocks rajas' effort, and sleep is a sinking into ignorance that stops the work of both.
Darkness draws people to sleep, sloth, intoxication and violence, dulls their sense of right and wrong, and makes them forget their spiritual identity and the chance human life offers.

verses.devanagari:
सत्त्वं सुखे सञ्जयति रजः कर्मणि भारत ।
ज्ञानमावृत्य तु तमः प्रमादे सञ्जयत्युत॥
verses.transliteration:
sattvaṃ sukhe sañjayati rajaḥ karmaṇi bhārata
jñānamāvṛtya tu tamaḥ pramāde sañjayatyuta
verses.essence: Sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action, Bharata; but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence.
verses.translation: Sattva attaches to happiness, Rajas to action, O Arjuna, while Tamas verily shrouding knowledge attaches to heedlessness.
verses.explanation: The summary table, one verb three ways: sañjayati, it attaches. Sattva glues you to feeling-good, rajas to doing, tamas — after first pulling the blind down over knowing — to not-caring. Notice the diagnostic gift: identify what you cannot stop reaching for, and you have identified which strand is currently holding the pen.
verses.connection: Compresses 14.6–8 into a field guide: three attachments, three rulers.
verses.reflection: Run the diagnostic at noon: what can I not stop reaching for right now? That names the ruler.
verses.background: The three strands are introduced by name and grip: sattva, rajas, tamas, born of prakriti, binding the imperishable dweller in the body — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by thirst and attachment to action, tamas by negligence, sloth, and sleep, veiling knowledge.
verses.hook: In a word, what does each of the three qualities attach you to?

views.text: The knowledge tamas veils is the discrimination that sattva produces; pramāda means failing to do the duty at hand.
Stresses each strand's overriding force: sattva keeps one turned toward happiness even amid causes of grief, and tamas veils even what the great teach; 'uta' adds that it also yokes one to laziness.
Goodness can breed complacency and intellectual pride, passion drives intense work that creates more karma, and darkness clouds judgment until people harm themselves for pleasure.

verses.devanagari:
रजस्तमश्चाभिभूय सत्त्वं भवति भारत ।
रजः सत्त्वं तमश्चैव तमः सत्त्वं रजस्तथा॥
verses.transliteration:
rajastamaścābhibhūya sattvaṃ bhavati bhārata
rajaḥ sattvaṃ tamaścaiva tamaḥ sattvaṃ rajastathā
verses.essence: Sattva prevails, Bharata, overpowering rajas and tamas; rajas, overpowering sattva and tamas; and tamas, overpowering sattva and rajas.
verses.translation: Now Sattva arises (prevails), O Arjuna, having overpowered Rajas and Tamas; nor Rajas, having overpowered Sattva and Tamas; and now Tamas, having overpowered Sattva and Rajas.
verses.explanation: The inner weather report: the three are never absent, only in shifting majority — each rises abhibhūya, by *overpowering* the other two. A single day cycles through all three governments: the clear morning, the driven afternoon, the leaden evening. The self watches a parliament it did not elect form and fall, hour by hour.
verses.connection: The dynamics: 14.6–9's strands as rivals in perpetual coup — observable in any afternoon.
verses.reflection: Watch one full cycle today — clear morning, driven afternoon, heavy evening — as governments changing.
verses.background: The strands are shown contending for government: now sattva prevails over rajas and tamas, now rajas, now tamas — and the field signs of each ruler are given: light at all the body's gates when sattva reigns; greed, restlessness, and craving under rajas; darkness, inertia, and delusion under tamas.
verses.hook: Why do your moods keep shifting between calm, drive and dullness?

views.text: Each quality grows by subduing the other two and then produces its own effects: sattva knowledge and happiness, rajas activity and hankering, tamas the obscuring of knowledge.
All three are always present in the embodied self; which one rises or is subdued depends on past karma and on the food that nourishes the body.
Each strand has its turn, like seasons succeeding one another; the means of strengthening sattva are taught later in chapters 17 and 18.
Like three wrestlers taking turns on top, the qualities keep overpowering one another in the mind, depending on surroundings, thoughts and past tendencies, so one's temperament swings among them.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वद्वारेषु देहेऽस्मिन्प्रकाश उपजायते ।
ज्ञानं यदा तदा विद्याद्विवृद्धं सत्त्वमित्युत॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvadvāreṣu dehe'sminprakāśa upajāyate
jñānaṃ yadā tadā vidyādvivṛddhaṃ sattvamityuta
verses.essence: When through all the gates of this body the light of understanding shines forth — then one may know that sattva has increased.
verses.translation: When through every gate (sense) in this body, the wisdom-light shines, then it may be known that Sattva is predominant.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + द्वार (door): "all the doors"

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, locative singular (agrees with देहे)
noun, neuter, nominative singular (in apposition to प्रकाशः)

verses.explanation: The diagnostics begin — how to read which strand is ruling. Sattva's sign: prakāśa at sarva-dvāreṣu, light at *all* the gates — the nine doors of 5.13 now windows. Perception crisp, words clean, the world arriving in focus. When everything simply seems clearer, that is not the world improving; that is sattva ascendant.
verses.connection: First entry in the field-manual (14.11–13): sattva announced by clarity at the senses.
verses.reflection: Notice an hour when all the gates are lit — perception crisp, words clean — and thank sattva by name.
verses.background: The strands are shown contending for government: now sattva prevails over rajas and tamas, now rajas, now tamas — and the field signs of each ruler are given: light at all the body's gates when sattva reigns; greed, restlessness, and craving under rajas; darkness, inertia, and delusion under tamas.
verses.hook: How can you tell when goodness is rising in you?

views.text: Prakāśa is a function of the inner organ, intelligence, and that is what 'knowledge' means here; the ear and other senses are the Self's doors of perception.
The light is knowledge of sound and the other objects arising at every sense; the word 'uta' hints that sattva's rise is also known by happiness and its other signs.
Stand as a doorkeeper of the mind and let only sattvic thoughts pass; sattvic food, japa, meditation and holy company increase sattva.
The qualities even shape our attitude to spiritual practice; when goodness rises we feel eager to progress, and practice means holding the mind to devotion whatever quality prevails.

verses.devanagari:
लोभः प्रवृत्तिरारम्भः कर्मणामशमः स्पृहा ।
रजस्येतानि जायन्ते विवृद्धे भरतर्षभ॥
verses.transliteration:
lobhaḥ pravṛttirārambhaḥ karmaṇāmaśamaḥ spṛhā
rajasyetāni jāyante vivṛddhe bharatarṣabha
verses.essence: Greed, busyness, the undertaking of works, restlessness, craving — these arise, best of Bharatas, when rajas has increased.
verses.translation: Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, longing these arise when Rajas is predominant, O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + शम (calm): "absence of calm"

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (when, with विवृद्धे)
past participle, neuter, locative singular (when ... has increased)

anvaya.parts: भरत (Bharata) + ऋषभ (bull): "bull, chief of the Bharatas"

verses.explanation: Rajas's five tells, each recognizable from the inside: lobha, the more-hunger; pravṛtti, the compulsion to be in motion; ārambha, the launching of project after project; aśama, the inability to sit; spṛhā, the reflexive reaching. A culture can be read with this verse as easily as a mood — and modernity reads rajasic on every line.
verses.connection: Second entry: rajas announced not by feeling but by the calendar filling itself.
verses.reflection: Read your calendar as a symptom today: greed, launching, restlessness — rajas writes in appointments.
verses.background: The strands are shown contending for government: now sattva prevails over rajas and tamas, now rajas, now tamas — and the field signs of each ruler are given: light at all the body's gates when sattva reigns; greed, restlessness, and craving under rajas; darkness, inertia, and delusion under tamas.
verses.hook: What signs show that passion has taken hold of you?

views.text: When rajas predominates there arise avarice, the desire to take others' possessions; activity in general; undertaking of actions; unrest, shown as joy and attachment; and hankering, desire in general for all things.
Lobha is unwillingness to spend what one has; pravṛtti is activity with no purpose; ārambha is taking up works for their fruits; aśama is the senses never resting.
Aśama is the unceasing round of plans, 'having done this I will do that'; ārambha is the drive to build houses and the like; spṛhā is grabbing at whatever one sees.
Do not mistake rajasic bustle for karma yoga; motives usually hide personal desire, and the sage sitting still is in truth the most active.
Passion breeds greed and restless striving, even telling us spiritual progress can wait; we should not be dejected by such swings but use the intellect to keep the mind on God.

verses.devanagari:
अप्रकाशोऽप्रवृत्तिश्च प्रमादो मोह एव च ।
तमस्येतानि जायन्ते विवृद्धे कुरुनन्दन॥
verses.transliteration:
aprakāśo'pravṛttiśca pramādo moha eva ca
tamasyetāni jāyante vivṛddhe kurunandana
verses.essence: Darkness, inertia, negligence, and delusion — these arise, Kurunandana, when tamas has increased.
verses.translation: Darkness, inertness, heedlessness and delusion these arise when Tamas is predominant, O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + प्रकाश (light): "absence of light"
अ (not) + प्रवृत्ति (activity): "absence of activity"

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (when, with विवृद्धे)
past participle, neuter, locative singular (when ... has increased)

anvaya.base: कुरुनन्दन · delight of the Kuru line
anvaya.parts: कुरु (Kuru) + नन्दन (joy, son): "joy of the Kurus"

verses.explanation: Tamas diagnosed by negation: aprakāśa, the lights dimmed; apravṛtti, the engine that will not turn; then pramāda and moha, the slide from not-doing into not-seeing-why-it-matters. The danger is its self-concealment — sattva and rajas can notice themselves; tamas, by definition, has trouble noticing anything.
verses.connection: Third entry completes the manual — and 14.14–15 asks: which strand will you die in?
verses.reflection: Be alert for the strand that hides itself: when nothing seems to matter, that is tamas, mattering.
verses.background: The strands are shown contending for government: now sattva prevails over rajas and tamas, now rajas, now tamas — and the field signs of each ruler are given: light at all the body's gates when sattva reigns; greed, restlessness, and craving under rajas; darkness, inertia, and delusion under tamas.
verses.hook: What signs show that dullness and darkness are taking over?

views.text: Aprakāśa is complete loss of discrimination; negligence and delusion, a form of stupidity, are its effects.
Tamas is often mistaken for peace: 'all is prārabdha, all is māyā, why should I work, I am Brahman' is not spirituality but thick tamas.
Under darkness the mind doubts God and sees no point in practice; such fluctuation is natural, and steady practice, like learning to drive, makes rising above it easier.

verses.devanagari:
यदा सत्त्वे प्रवृद्धे तु प्रलयं याति देहभृत् ।
तदोत्तमविदां लोकानमलान्प्रतिपद्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yadā sattve pravṛddhe tu pralayaṃ yāti dehabhṛt
tadottamavidāṃ lokānamalānpratipadyate
verses.essence: When the embodied one meets dissolution while sattva prevails, then one attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.
verses.translation: If the embodied one meets with death when Sattva is predominant, then he attains to the spotless worlds of the knowers of the Highest.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (when, with प्रवृद्धे)
past participle, neuter, locative singular (when ... has grown)
noun, masculine, accusative singular (goal of motion)

anvaya.parts: देह (body) + भृत् (bearer): "one who bears a body"
उत्तम (highest) + विद् (knower): "those who know the highest"
अ (not) + मल (stain): "stainless"

verses.explanation: The strands follow past the body: die on a sattva tide, and the momentum carries to amalān lokān, stainless worlds, the company of the wise. Not a judgment passed from outside — just physics: the quality of consciousness at the moment of release is a trajectory, and trajectories continue. Chapter 8's final-thought doctrine, restated in guna terms.
verses.connection: Begins the death-accounting (14.14–15): the ruling strand as the soul's launch angle.
verses.reflection: Practice dying well by living well today: the tide you cultivate is the tide that carries.
verses.background: The strands follow the soul to the door of death and past it: dying in sattva, one reaches the pure worlds of the knowers; in rajas, birth among the action-bound; in tamas, the wombs of the deluded. Fruit follows seed — purity, pain, ignorance — and the directions: upward go the sattvic, the rajasic stand midway, downward the tamasic.
verses.hook: Where does someone go who dies while goodness prevails?

views.text: Tu means 'exclusively', when sattva alone prevails; the stainless worlds are those like Brahmā's, belonging to those who know principles such as mahat.
The pure worlds mean birth in families of those who know the self, where one becomes fit for the acts that lead to self-knowledge.
What counts is sattva cultivated through the whole of life, not a chance mood at the last moment, since at death delusion overtakes everyone.
We get what we deserve: those who cultivated virtue and service are reborn among the pious and learned or in higher realms.

verses.devanagari:
रजसि प्रलयं गत्वा कर्मसङ्गिषु जायते ।
तथा प्रलीनस्तमसि मूढयोनिषु जायते॥
verses.transliteration:
rajasi pralayaṃ gatvā karmasaṅgiṣu jāyate
tathā pralīnastamasi mūḍhayoniṣu jāyate
verses.essence: Meeting dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action; and dissolved in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
verses.translation: Meeting death in Rajas, he is born among those who are attached to action; and dying in Tamas, he is born in the womb of the senseless.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, accusative singular (goal of motion)

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + सङ्गिन् (attached one): "those attached to action"

anvaya.base: मूढयोनि · womb of a dull being
anvaya.parts: मूढ (deluded, dull) + योनि (womb): "wombs of the deluded"

verses.explanation: The other two launch angles: a rajasic death lands among karma-saṅgis — the driven, the striving, another lifetime on the wheel of doing; a tamasic one sinks toward mūḍha-yonis, births where delusion is the native air. No tribunal anywhere in the verse: like settles toward like, water finding its level across lifetimes.
verses.connection: Completes 14.14: three deaths, three gravities — motive enough for the cultivation 14.16–18 maps.
verses.reflection: Let like-settles-toward-like motivate one upgrade today — no tribunal, just trajectory.
verses.background: The strands follow the soul to the door of death and past it: dying in sattva, one reaches the pure worlds of the knowers; in rajas, birth among the action-bound; in tamas, the wombs of the deluded. Fruit follows seed — purity, pain, ignorance — and the directions: upward go the sattvic, the rajasic stand midway, downward the tamasic.
verses.hook: What birth follows a death in passion or in darkness?

views.text: Dying while rajas predominates, one is born among human beings attached to work; dying while tamas predominates, among stupid species such as animals.
A rajasic death brings birth among those who act for their own gain, fit for rites that win heaven; a tamasic one brings wombs like those of dogs and pigs, unable to pursue any human end.
Reads the verse as the fruit of a whole life: rajasic living earns a human birth of mixed experience, tamasic living births in hells, animals and trees; he rejects tying it to the last moment alone.
Records a softer view some hold: the 'deluded womb' may be birth among the dullest humans, not necessarily an animal body.
Human birth is not guaranteed: the greedy are reborn among the worldly busy, and the lazy or violent may even slide back into animal forms.

verses.devanagari:
कर्मणः सुकृतस्याहुः सात्त्विकं निर्मलं फलम् ।
रजसस्तु फलं दुःखमज्ञानं तमसः फलम्॥
verses.transliteration:
karmaṇaḥ sukṛtasyāhuḥ sāttvikaṃ nirmalaṃ phalam
rajasastu phalaṃ duḥkhamajñānaṃ tamasaḥ phalam
verses.essence: Of good action, they say, the fruit is sattvic and stainless; the fruit of rajas is pain; and ignorance is the fruit of tamas.
verses.translation: The fruit of good action, they say, is Sattvic and pure, verily the fruit of Rajas is pain, and ignorance is the fruit of Tamas.

anvaya.parts: सु (well) + कृत (done): "well done"

anvaya.form: verb, perfect with present sense, 3rd person plural

anvaya.parts: निस् (without) + मल (stain): "stainless"

verses.explanation: The harvest table: sattvic action ripens clean; rajasic action — whatever it wins — ripens as duḥkha, since craving's victories arrive pre-loaded with the next craving; tamasic action ripens as deeper ajñāna, ignorance compounding like a debt. Each strand pays its workers in its own currency, and the currency is more of itself.
verses.connection: The fruit-ledger that 14.17 traces back to its psychological roots.
verses.reflection: Check the harvest, not the seed packet, tonight: what did today's actions actually ripen into?
verses.background: The strands follow the soul to the door of death and past it: dying in sattva, one reaches the pure worlds of the knowers; in rajas, birth among the action-bound; in tamas, the wombs of the deluded. Fruit follows seed — purity, pain, ignorance — and the directions: upward go the sattvic, the rajasic stand midway, downward the tamasic.
verses.hook: What kind of fruit does each quality's action bear?

views.text: Since the topic is action, 'rajas' and 'tamas' here mean rajasic and tamasic acts; each result matches its cause, so rajasic work yields sorrow and unrighteous tamasic work yields ignorance.
The good deed is disinterested work done as worship of the Lord; dying in sattva it brings birth among knowers of the self, where sattva grows further and the self becomes purer.
Holds that verses 16 to 20 are later insertions that only repeat what came before and should be set aside; living beyond the strands is itself emancipation.
Pure-minded action in goodness yields uplifting results, action in passion feeds sensual craving and so brings pain, and action in darkness, disregarding scripture, deepens delusion.

verses.devanagari:
सत्त्वात्सञ्जायते ज्ञानं रजसो लोभ एव च ।
प्रमादमोहौ तमसो भवतोऽज्ञानमेव च॥
verses.transliteration:
sattvātsañjāyate jñānaṃ rajaso lobha eva ca
pramādamohau tamaso bhavato'jñānameva ca
verses.essence: From sattva arises knowledge, and from rajas, greed; from tamas arise negligence and delusion — and ignorance too.
verses.translation: From Sattva arises knowledge, and greed from Rajas; heedlessness and delusion arise from Tamas, and also ignorance.

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, nominative dual (the two)
anvaya.parts: प्रमाद (negligence) + मोह (delusion): a pair joined by 'and'

verses.explanation: The strands as factories, each with one product line: sattva manufactures jñāna, knowing; rajas manufactures lobha, the wanting of more; tamas runs three shifts — negligence, delusion, ignorance. The practical inference is the chapter's quiet gift: to get more knowledge, do not chase knowledge; cultivate the strand that produces it.
verses.connection: The production chain behind 14.16's fruits — quality of being precedes quality of mind.
verses.reflection: Want more knowledge? Do not chase it today — cultivate the strand that manufactures it.
verses.background: The strands follow the soul to the door of death and past it: dying in sattva, one reaches the pure worlds of the knowers; in rajas, birth among the action-bound; in tamas, the wombs of the deluded. Fruit follows seed — purity, pain, ignorance — and the directions: upward go the sattvic, the rajasic stand midway, downward the tamasic.
verses.hook: What does each of the three qualities give rise to in the mind?

views.text: When sattva predominates, knowledge is born; from rajas comes avarice; and from tamas come inadvertence, delusion and also ignorance.
Sattva yields direct knowledge of the self, rajas a craving for heaven and the like; tamas runs a chain, negligence into evil acts, then wrong knowledge, more tamas, and finally no knowledge at all.
Gives this as the reason behind 14.16: because sattva produces knowledge, sattvic action bears bright, happy fruit, and because greed brings sorrow, rajasic action bears pain.
Goodness gives discernment and contentment, passion inflames the senses with ambitious desire, and darkness shrouds a person in inertia that leads to wicked deeds.

verses.devanagari:
ऊर्ध्वं गच्छन्ति सत्त्वस्था मध्ये तिष्ठन्ति राजसाः ।
जघन्यगुणवृत्तिस्था अधो गच्छन्ति तामसाः॥
verses.transliteration:
ūrdhvaṃ gacchanti sattvasthā madhye tiṣṭhanti rājasāḥ
jaghanyaguṇavṛttisthā adho gacchanti tāmasāḥ
verses.essence: Those established in sattva go upward; the rajasic remain in the middle; the tamasic, abiding in the lowest tendency, go downward.
verses.translation: Those who are seated in Sattva go upwards; the Rajasic dwell in the middle; and the Tamasic, abiding in the function of the lowest Guna, go downwards.

anvaya.parts: सत्त्व (sattva) + स्थ (standing in): "those who abide in sattva"

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural

anvaya.meaning: abiding in the lowest strand's ways
anvaya.base: जघन्यगुणवृत्तिस्थ · living by the lowest guna
anvaya.parts: जघन्य (lowest) + गुण (strand) + वृत्ति (mode, conduct) + स्थ (abiding): "those who live in the workings of the lowest strand"

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural

verses.explanation: The whole cosmology as a single elevator: ūrdhvam, madhye, adhaḥ — up, level, down. The strands are not moral categories but densities, and beings sort by buoyancy. Yet the verse describes a treadmill even at its top: 'upward' is still *within* the three-strand machine. The next verse opens the door out of the building entirely.
verses.connection: The vertical map of the guna-world — drawn so 14.19 can point beyond all three floors.
verses.reflection: Locate your floor honestly this evening — rising, level, or sinking — then look for the stairwell out.
verses.background: The strands follow the soul to the door of death and past it: dying in sattva, one reaches the pure worlds of the knowers; in rajas, birth among the action-bound; in tamas, the wombs of the deluded. Fruit follows seed — purity, pain, ignorance — and the directions: upward go the sattvic, the rajasic stand midway, downward the tamasic.
verses.hook: Which way does each quality carry a person: up, middle or down?

refs.note: Those in goodness reach heaven, those in passion return to earth, those in darkness go to lower worlds, and those beyond the qualities reach God.

views.text: Upward means birth among gods, middle among humans, down among cattle; all this guna-bound wandering is false knowledge rooted in ignorance, so liberation must come from right knowledge, taught next.
Those in sattva rise toward release from saṃsāra by degrees; the tamasic sink step by step, through animals and insects down to plants, stones and clods of earth.
The upward path is graded, each higher world holding a hundredfold more joy up to Satyaloka; the rajasic are reborn among humans, the tamasic in hells such as Tāmisra.
Like students admitted to colleges by their grades, souls are reborn in realms matching the quality that dominated their lives.

verses.devanagari:
नान्यं गुणेभ्यः कर्तारं यदा द्रष्टानुपश्यति ।
गुणेभ्यश्च परं वेत्ति मद्भावं सोऽधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
nānyaṃ guṇebhyaḥ kartāraṃ yadā draṣṭānupaśyati
guṇebhyaśca paraṃ vetti madbhāvaṃ so'dhigacchati
verses.essence: When the seer beholds no doer other than the gunas, and knows That which is beyond the gunas — one attains my being.
verses.translation: When the seer beholds no agent other than the Gunas and knows That which is higher than they, he attains to My Being.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, accusative singular (object)

anvaya.parts: मद् (my) + भाव (being, state): "my being"

verses.explanation: The exit, in two recognitions. First, nānyaṁ guṇebhyaḥ kartāram: all doing, every act ever performed, is strand acting on strand; the 'doer' was the gunas wearing a name. Second, the seer knows the param, what stands beyond the weave as its witness. Draṣṭā, the watcher, is the one role no strand can play. This is the chapter's moksha-verse, the seeing that 3.27 planted and 13.30 watered, now bearing fruit, and its arrival is named mad-bhāvam, his own being. Watch the weather long enough as weather, and you discover you are the sky.
verses.connection: The liberating insight: 3.27 and 13.30 fused — and crowned with arrival in his being.
verses.reflection: Say the freeing sentence over one strong mood today: no doer here but the strands — and watch from the sky.
verses.background: The chapter's verses of release: when the seer beholds no doer other than the strands and knows what is higher than the strands, he attains My being — transcending the three that birthed the body, freed from birth, death, old age, and pain, he tastes immortality.
verses.hook: What does the seer understand that brings him to Krishna's own nature?

views.text: Once illumined, the witness sees the strands, transformed into body, organs and objects, as the only agents, and knows the witness beyond them as himself; that is attaining the Lord's nature.
First one must settle in pure sattva through sattvic food and actions offered to the Lord; then, seeing the self as non-agent and pure knowledge, one gains likeness to him, not identity.
The qualities are the doers in the world, but God and everything of his are beyond them; attaching the mind to him through devotion lifts it above the qualities.

verses.devanagari:
गुणानेतानतीत्य त्रीन्देही देहसमुद्भवान् ।
जन्ममृत्युजरादुःखैर्विमुक्तोऽमृतमश्नुते॥
verses.transliteration:
guṇānetānatītya trīndehī dehasamudbhavān
janmamṛtyujarāduḥkhairvimukto'mṛtamaśnute
verses.essence: Transcending these three gunas, which are the source of the body, the embodied one — released from birth, death, old age and sorrow — attains immortality.
verses.translation: The embodied one having crossed beyond these three Gunas out of which the body is evolved, is freed from birth, death, decay and pain, and attains to immortality.

anvaya.base: देहिन् · one who has a body

anvaya.parts: देह (body) + समुद्भव (origin): "which give rise to the body"

anvaya.meaning: from birth, death, old age, sorrow
anvaya.form: noun compound, neuter, instrumental plural (from, with 'freed')
anvaya.parts: जन्म (birth) + मृत्यु (death) + जरा (old age) + दुःख (sorrow): a list joined by 'and'

verses.explanation: The full prize: the gunas are deha-samudbhavān, the very loom the body is woven on — step past them and the whole production line of embodiment, with its fixed menu of birth-death-age-sorrow, loses its claim. Amṛtam aśnute: one reaches and enjoys deathlessness, the same phrase as 13.13 — liberation as something lived, not theory.
verses.connection: States the stakes of 14.19's seeing — and provokes Arjuna's immediate, practical question.
verses.reflection: Taste the full stakes once: past the three strands lies freedom from the body's whole fixed menu.
verses.background: The chapter's verses of release: when the seer beholds no doer other than the strands and knows what is higher than the strands, he attains My being — transcending the three that birthed the body, freed from birth, death, old age, and pain, he tastes immortality.
verses.hook: What is gained by going beyond the three qualities of nature?

views.text: The transcending happens even while living: the enlightened one goes beyond the strands that make up māyā and the body's seed, and is free from birth, death and sorrow in this very life.
Crossing the strands means seeing the self as other than them and made of knowledge alone; experiencing that immortal self is what 'likeness to Me' means.
Takes amṛta as the bliss of Brahman, reached once every harm the strands cause has ceased, so the person has done all there is to do.
Even goodness is a chain, though of gold; only by transcending all three qualities does the soul escape birth, disease, old age and death and taste the immortality it longs for.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
कैर्लिङ्गैस्त्रीन्गुणानेतानतीतो भवति प्रभो ।
किमाचारः कथं चैतांस्त्रीन्गुणानतिवर्तते॥
verses.transliteration:
kairliṅgaistrīnguṇānetānatīto bhavati prabho
kimācāraḥ kathaṃ caitāṃstrīnguṇānativartate
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: by what marks is one known who has gone beyond these three gunas, O Lord? What is such a one's conduct? And how does one pass beyond these three gunas?
verses.translation: What are the marks of him who has transcended the three qualities, O Lord? What is his conduct and how does he go beyond these three qualities?

anvaya.parts: किम् (what) + आचार (conduct): "one whose conduct is what?"

verses.explanation: Arjuna's recurring question — he asked it of the sthita-prajña in 2.54 — returns for the guṇātīta: how would I recognize one? how do they live? how is it done? The repetition is the Gita's pedagogy: every metaphysical summit must be brought down to gait and gesture, or it remains decoration.
verses.connection: Echoes 2.54's question: the demand for a walking, breathing portrait of 14.20's freed one.
verses.reflection: Ask Arjuna's practical question of every ideal you meet: how is it recognized, lived, and reached?
verses.background: Arjuna asks the practical question — by what marks is the one beyond the strands known, and how does he cross them? Krishna gives the gunatita portrait: hating nothing that comes, craving nothing that ceases, seated as one unconcerned while the strands turn, equal in clod, stone, and gold — and then the method that overturns the chapter's analytics: unswerving devotion to Me carries one across, for I am the very foundation of Brahman, of immortality, and of absolute bliss.
verses.hook: How can you recognise someone who has gone beyond the three qualities?

views.text: Arjuna asks two things, the signs of one beyond the strands and the means of going beyond them, and the Lord's reply answers both in turn.
Behind the question is a doubt: anyone with a body lives in some mental state, and every such state belongs to one of the strands, so how can an embodied person transcend them?
Calling Krishna 'Prabhu' hints that he alone, like a king relieving his servants, can remove Arjuna's sorrow; the marks of the freed sage are also what seekers should cultivate.
Arjun asks three things: the signs of one beyond the qualities, how such a person behaves, and how one transcends them, which Krishna answers in order.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
प्रकाशं च प्रवृत्तिं च मोहमेव च पाण्डव ।
न द्वेष्टि सम्प्रवृत्तानि न निवृत्तानि काङ्क्षति॥
verses.transliteration:
prakāśaṃ ca pravṛttiṃ ca mohameva ca pāṇḍava
na dveṣṭi sampravṛttāni na nivṛttāni kāṅkṣati
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: one who does not hate illumination, activity and delusion when they arise, Pandava, nor longs for them when they cease —
verses.translation: When light, activity and delusion are present, he hates them not, nor does he long for them when they are absent.

anvaya.form: past participle, neuter, accusative plural (them, as arisen)
past participle, neuter, accusative plural (them, as ceased)

verses.explanation: The answer's first surprise: the transcender does not hate even *tamas*. Prakāśa, pravṛtti, moha — sattva's light, rajas's drive, tamas's fog — arrive and depart like weather, and the guṇātīta neither resents the storm nor pines for the sun. Fighting a guna is done *with* a guna; only the unresisting watcher stands outside the game.
verses.connection: Begins the gunatita-portrait (14.22–25): transcendence as the end of the inner argument with one's own states.
verses.reflection: Practice non-hatred of your own states today — even the fog. Fighting a guna is done with a guna.
verses.background: Arjuna asks the practical question — by what marks is the one beyond the strands known, and how does he cross them? Krishna gives the gunatita portrait: hating nothing that comes, craving nothing that ceases, seated as one unconcerned while the strands turn, equal in clod, stone, and gold — and then the method that overturns the chapter's analytics: unswerving devotion to Me carries one across, for I am the very foundation of Brahman, of immortality, and of absolute bliss.
verses.hook: Does a free person resist or crave light, activity and confusion?

views.text: The unenlightened resent their states: 'tamas has deluded me', 'rajas has pulled me from my nature'. This mark is purely inward; dislike and longing are felt by oneself and cannot be seen by others.
The indifference concerns things other than the self. Disliking what hinders self-realisation and longing for what helps it are not ruled out by this verse.
Light, activity and delusion remain in everyone as marks of the body. The yogi neither rejoices in them nor hates them, reflecting that they belong to the body and cannot disturb him.
Arjuna is asking again what 2.54 already answered, wanting more detail, so the reply comes in six verses. This one gives the inward mark; the sentence completes in 14.25 with 'he is called gunatita'.
The illumined are not disturbed by the qualities at work in the world or even in their own minds; they see the mind as separate from themselves and refuse thoughts that harm devotion.

verses.devanagari:
उदासीनवदासीनो गुणैर्यो न विचाल्यते ।
गुणा वर्तन्त इत्येव योऽवतिष्ठति नेङ्गते॥
verses.transliteration:
udāsīnavadāsīno guṇairyo na vicālyate
guṇā vartanta ityeva yo'vatiṣṭhati neṅgate
verses.essence: Seated as one indifferent, unshaken by the gunas; 'the gunas are operating' — knowing thus, one stands firm and does not waver.
verses.translation: He who, seated like one unconcerned, is not moved by the qualities, and who, knowing that the qualities are active, is self-centred and moves not.

anvaya.base: उदासीन · one sitting apart, neutral + वत् · like
anvaya.parts: उदासीन (neutral onlooker) + वत् (like): 'as a neutral would'

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (one sitting)
verb, causative passive, present, 3rd person singular (is made to move)

verses.explanation: The inner posture, with its mantra included: guṇā vartanta iti — 'strands are turning.' Mood arrives: strands turning. Energy crashes: strands turning. The attribution does all the work, the same move as 3.28, now a settled stance. Udāsīna-vat, *as if* uninvolved: present, perceiving everything, contracted to nothing. Na iṅgate — the windless lamp of 6.19, returned.
verses.connection: The watcher's stance — 14.19's insight worn as a daily posture.
verses.reflection: Use the mantra at the next mood swing: gunah vartante — strands are turning — and do not stir.
verses.background: Arjuna asks the practical question — by what marks is the one beyond the strands known, and how does he cross them? Krishna gives the gunatita portrait: hating nothing that comes, craving nothing that ceases, seated as one unconcerned while the strands turn, equal in clod, stone, and gold — and then the method that overturns the chapter's analytics: unswerving devotion to Me carries one across, for I am the very foundation of Brahman, of immortality, and of absolute bliss.
verses.text_note: Variant: ity evaṃ for ity eva.
verses.hook: How does one beyond the qualities stay steady while they act?

views.text: He is not pulled from the knowledge born of discrimination. He sees the gunas, become body, senses and objects, acting on one another; any outward activity is merely the momentum of actions already cancelled by insight.
He sits unconcerned because his satisfaction lies in seeing the self as different from the gunas. 'Rests unshaken' means he does not act in line with what the gunas produce.
With this verse the marks others can see begin, answering 'how does he behave?'. Udāsīnavat means seated as a witness, discerning 'the gunas move in their own work; I have no connection with them.'
Knowing that only the qualities are acting, such a person stays like a witness, helps the world from their nature, leaves results to God, and distances themselves from the mind's negative thoughts.

verses.devanagari:
समदुःखसुखः स्वस्थः समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः ।
तुल्यप्रियाप्रियो धीरस्तुल्यनिन्दात्मसंस्तुतिः॥
verses.transliteration:
samaduḥkhasukhaḥ svasthaḥ samaloṣṭāśmakāñcanaḥ
tulyapriyāpriyo dhīrastulyanindātmasaṃstutiḥ
verses.essence: Alike in sorrow and joy, abiding in the self; alike toward a clod, a stone and gold; equal toward the dear and the undear; steady; equal in blame and in praise of oneself —
verses.translation: Who is the same in pleasure and pain, who dwells in the Self, to whom a clod of earth, stone and gold are alike, who is the same to the dear and the unfriendly, who is firm, and to whom censure and praise are as one.

anvaya.meaning: to whom sorrow and joy are alike
anvaya.base: सम · same, equal; दुःख · sorrow; सुख · joy
anvaya.parts: सम (equal) + दुःख (sorrow) + सुख (joy): 'one for whom sorrow and joy are equal'
स्व (one's own self) + स्थ (standing in): 'one who stands in himself'

anvaya.meaning: to whom clod, stone, gold are alike
anvaya.base: सम · equal; लोष्ट · clod; अश्मन् · stone; काञ्चन · gold
anvaya.parts: सम (equal) + लोष्ट (clod) + अश्म (stone) + काञ्चन (gold): 'one for whom clod, stone and gold are equal'

anvaya.base: तुल्य · equal; प्रिय · dear; अप्रिय · not dear
anvaya.parts: तुल्य (equal) + प्रिय (pleasant) + अप्रिय (unpleasant): 'one for whom pleasant and unpleasant are equal'

anvaya.base: तुल्य · equal; निन्दा · blame; आत्मन् · self; संस्तुति · praise
anvaya.parts: तुल्य (equal) + निन्दा (blame) + आत्म (of oneself) + संस्तुति (praise): 'one for whom blame and praise of himself are equal'

verses.explanation: The equality-list returns from 6.8 and 12.18, with one word doing new work: sva-sthaḥ — *standing in one's own self*, self-stationed. That is the secret of all the samenesses that surround it: clod and gold weigh the same only to one whose footing depends on neither. The evenness is not effort; it is residence.
verses.connection: The portrait's center: every 'equal' in the list flows from one address — svastha.
verses.reflection: Stand in yourself once today — svastha — and let clod, stone, and gold briefly weigh the same.
verses.background: Arjuna asks the practical question — by what marks is the one beyond the strands known, and how does he cross them? Krishna gives the gunatita portrait: hating nothing that comes, craving nothing that ceases, seated as one unconcerned while the strands turn, equal in clod, stone, and gold — and then the method that overturns the chapter's analytics: unswerving devotion to Me carries one across, for I am the very foundation of Brahman, of immortality, and of absolute bliss.
verses.hook: How does such a person regard pleasure, pain, gold and earth?

views.text: 'Svastha' is glossed as established in one's own Self, tranquil; such a wise monk finds sorrow and happiness, earth, iron and gold, the agreeable and disagreeable, and censure and praise of himself all the same.

Love for the self keeps him even amid the births and deaths of relatives. Dhīra means skilled in telling prakṛti from the self, so praise and blame are seen as belonging to body-identification, not to him.
Svastha is the cause of the rest: joy and sorrow are equal to him because he is settled in his own nature. Dear and undear are taken as the causes of joy and sorrow; dhīra means intelligent.
As day and night mean nothing to a post fixed in the ground, pleasure and pain mean nothing to the sage who dwells in the Self; cowdung and gold, a jewel and a stone, are of equal value to him.
Established in the self, which like God is beyond the qualities, the realized person sees the world's dualities without being moved, regarding stone, earth and gold alike.

verses.devanagari:
मानापमानयोस्तुल्यस्तुल्यो मित्रारिपक्षयोः ।
सर्वारम्भपरित्यागी गुणातीतः स उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
mānāpamānayostulyastulyo mitrāripakṣayoḥ
sarvārambhaparityāgī guṇātītaḥ sa ucyate
verses.essence: — alike in honor and dishonor, alike toward the sides of friend and foe, renouncing all self-serving undertakings: that one is said to have gone beyond the gunas.
verses.translation: Who is the same in honour and dishonour, the same to friend and foe, abandoning all undertakings he is said to have transcended the qualities.

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, locative dual (in both)
anvaya.parts: मान (honour) + अपमान (dishonour): 'honour and dishonour', a pair

anvaya.meaning: toward the sides of friend and foe
anvaya.base: मित्र · friend; अरि · enemy; पक्ष · side, party
anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, locative dual (toward both)
anvaya.parts: मित्र (friend) + अरि (foe) + पक्ष (side): 'the friend's side and the foe's side'

anvaya.base: सर्व · all; आरम्भ · undertaking; परित्यागिन् · one who gives up
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + आरम्भ (undertaking) + परित्यागी (abandoner): 'one who gives up all undertakings'
गुण (the strands) + अतीत (passed beyond): 'one who has passed beyond the gunas'

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: The portrait completes on Arjuna's exact wound: tulyo mitrāri-pakṣayoḥ — alike toward the *sides*, the pakṣa, friend's army and foe's. The man paralyzed in chapter 1 by which side held whom is shown a being for whom the sides have lost their pull. Guṇātītaḥ sa ucyate: the title conferred — and 14.26 will reveal the one practice that earns it.
verses.connection: Seals the portrait with the battlefield word 'paksha' — then the chapter springs its devotional turn.
verses.reflection: Feel the pull of the sides today — friend's and foe's — and practice one minute beyond both.
verses.background: Arjuna asks the practical question — by what marks is the one beyond the strands known, and how does he cross them? Krishna gives the gunatita portrait: hating nothing that comes, craving nothing that ceases, seated as one unconcerned while the strands turn, equal in clod, stone, and gold — and then the method that overturns the chapter's analytics: unswerving devotion to Me carries one across, for I am the very foundation of Brahman, of immortality, and of absolute bliss.
verses.hook: How does the free person treat honour, insult, friend and foe?

views.text: The traits from 14.23 to here are disciplines a monk seeking liberation practises with effort; once firmly ingrained they become his own inward marks. 'Undertakings' are acts aimed at seen or unseen results; he keeps only what maintains the body.

Honour and dishonour are feelings born of taking the body for the self. Seeing that body and self differ, he knows friend and foe have no real connection with him, and so gives up the enterprises of embodied life.
For 14.23 to 14.25 the means is one firm conviction: the exertion found in the body and senses is simply their own nature, and I am unconcerned with any fruit.
No longer identifying with the body's joys and sorrows, such a person meets praise and blame, favour and hostility with the same even vision.

verses.devanagari:
मां च योऽव्यभिचारेण भक्तियोगेन सेवते ।
स गुणान्समतीत्यैतान्ब्रह्मभूयाय कल्पते॥
verses.transliteration:
māṃ ca yo'vyabhicāreṇa bhaktiyogena sevate
sa guṇānsamatītyaitānbrahmabhūyāya kalpate
verses.essence: And one who serves me with the unswerving yoga of devotion — that one, passing beyond these gunas, becomes fit for the state of Brahman.
verses.translation: And he who serves Me with unswerving devotion, he, crossing beyond the qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman.

anvaya.form: noun compound used as adjective, masculine, instrumental singular (with)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + व्यभिचार (straying aside): 'that which never strays'
भक्ति (devotion) + योग (yoga): 'devotion that is itself the yoga'
ब्रह्म (Brahman) + भूय (becoming): 'the becoming of Brahman'

verses.explanation: Arjuna's third question, *how* does one cross?, is answered at last, and the answer reorganizes the chapter: not a technique of watching but a direction of loving. Mām ca yo 'vyabhicāreṇa bhakti-yogena sevate: whoever serves me with devotion that does not stray. The logic is exact: every effort to climb out of the gunas is made *of* gunas; only attachment to what is beyond them can draw one beyond them. Love is the single rope let down from outside the weave. Sa guṇān samatītyaitān, fully crossing these strands, brahma-bhūyāya kalpate: such a one becomes fit for the state of Brahman.
verses.connection: The chapter's resolution: the gunatita is made not by struggle against the strands but by devotion to their Lord.
verses.reflection: Use the one rope from outside the weave today: unswerving devotion — love your way past the strands.

verses.hook: What is Krishna's way to rise beyond the three qualities?

refs.note: When scripture calls God attributeless, it means free of material attributes; his personal form has infinite divine qualities, so devotion to it transcends the modes.

views.text: 'Me' is God, Nārāyaṇa dwelling in the hearts of all, and the server may be a monk or a man of action. Devotion is itself the yoga, and 'becoming Brahman' means liberation.

Reflecting on the difference between prakṛti and self is not enough, since beginningless impressions overturn it. Only one-pointed bhakti to the compassionate Lord crosses the otherwise invincible gunas; 'Brahman' here is the self in its true, immortal nature.

Ca means 'exclusively': whoever chases a fruit and keeps the Lord secondary is excluded. The true devotee, asked why he acts so, answers only with silent tears and thrilled body, purified by devotion that is the Lord's own grace.

Unswerving devotion is an unbroken flow of one thought of God, like oil poured from one vessel to another, with all thought of sense objects abandoned; this constant remembrance is the sure means of crossing the gunas.
Knowing the self is not enough; only fixing the mind on God's personal form through unwavering devotion makes it free of the qualities, and true transcendental meditation is meditation on him.

verses.devanagari:
ब्रह्मणो हि प्रतिष्ठाहममृतस्याव्ययस्य च ।
शाश्वतस्य च धर्मस्य सुखस्यैकान्तिकस्य च॥
verses.transliteration:
brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhāhamamṛtasyāvyayasya ca
śāśvatasya ca dharmasya sukhasyaikāntikasya ca
verses.essence: For I am the foundation of Brahman — of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss.
verses.translation: For I am the abode of Brahman, the immortal and the immutable, of everlasting Dharma and of absolute bliss.
verses.explanation: The chapter's last line inverts the expected hierarchy: brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhāham, for I am the *ground* on which Brahman stands. The immortal, the imperishable, the eternal dharma, absolute bliss: all listed, and the one speaking placed beneath them as their pedestal. The little word hi, 'for', makes this the reason behind 14.26: devotion to him carries one to Brahman because he is its foundation. Commentators part ways over what 'Brahman' and 'I' mean here, from the inmost Self as abode of the supreme Self to the individual self grounded in the Lord to Brahman condensed into form, but on every reading the inversion stuns: Brahman has a pedestal, and it speaks.
verses.connection: Seals 14.26's claim with the chapter's boldest theology — and hands the personal-God thread to chapter 15.
verses.reflection: Rest tonight on the foundation beneath even Brahman — the person this whole song is spoken by.

verses.hook: What is the ground on which the imperishable Brahman rests?

refs.note: The light from the toenails of Krishna's feet is the Brahman that sages and gods meditate on, so Krishna is its basis.
The effulgence of God's divine body is what the Upaniṣads call Brahman.

views.text: The inmost Self is the abode of the supreme Self, so through knowledge it is realised to be that Self. Alternatively, 'Brahman' is the conditioned Brahman, and the speaker, the unconditioned, is its ground.

'Brahman' here is the individual self, immortal and immutable, and 'eternal dharma' means the goal, not conduct. Because the Lord grounds self, prosperity and bliss, refuge in him is the only way past the gunas (as 7.14 says).
One becomes Brahman by serving the 'I'. Contemplating Brahman as bare, insentient being leads only to a release no different from deep sleep.
Pratiṣṭhā means image: 'I am Brahman condensed', as the sun's disk is light made solid. So one who serves him must come to his state, and 'fit for Brahman' is justified.
The formless Brahman worshipped by the knowers is the radiance of Krishna's personal form, so unwavering devotion to that form is the cure for bondage to the qualities.
